rule_link.how_it_backs: Justifies scoring rearfoot landing ahead of the center of mass as a braking/impact flaw: habitually barefoot forefoot strikers generate smaller collision forces than shod rearfoot strikers, so the feet_strike rule penalizes overstriding and cues landing closer under the body.

summary: Lieberman and colleagues compared foot-strike patterns and collision forces between habitually barefoot runners and habitually shod runners. Barefoot runners tended to forefoot- or midfoot-strike, while shod runners mostly rearfoot-strike. The forefoot-strike pattern produced smaller collision (impact-transient) forces than rearfoot striking in shoes. The authors conclude that the way the foot meets the ground — not barefoot-vs-shod per se — drives impact loading.
methods_signal: Observational + biomechanical comparison of habitually barefoot vs shod adult runners, combining foot-strike classification with force-plate collision-force measurement during running.

snippet.text: Landing on the forefoot with a compliant ankle avoids the sharp impact transient of a heel-first landing; runners who overstride onto the heel take the largest collision hit.
snippet.grounds_in: Paraphrase of Abstract + Results (collision-force comparison across strike types)

figure.what_it_shows: Side-view schematic: overstriding heel landing ahead of center of mass with a sharp vertical-force spike vs forefoot landing under the body with a blunted impact curve.
